subtopic: The Making of Nationalism in Europe
solution:
Giuseppe Mazzini was an Italian revolutionary and the most influential voice of nationalism in early-nineteenth-century Europe.

1. He was born in Genoa in 1805 and became a member of the secret society of the Carbonari.
2. As a young man of 24 he was sent into exile in 1831 for attempting a revolution in Liguria.
3. He founded two underground societies — Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne — whose members were like-minded young men from Poland, France, Italy and the German states.
4. He believed that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind, so Italy could not continue to be a patchwork of small states and kingdoms; it had to be forged into a single unified republic within a wider alliance of nations, and this unification alone could be the basis of Italian liberty.
5. Following his model, secret societies were set up in Germany, France, Switzerland and Poland. His opposition to monarchy frightened the conservatives, and Metternich described him as 'the most dangerous enemy of our social order'.
groundedIn: § 2 4 The Revolutionaries — the chapter's account of Mazzini: Genoa 1805, the Carbonari, exile in 1831, Young Italy and Young Europe, and Metternich's description of him

subtopic: The Making of Germany and Italy
solution:
Cavour was the Chief Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont who led the movement to unify the regions of Italy.

1. He was neither a revolutionary nor a democrat. Like many other wealthy and educated members of the Italian elite, he spoke French much better than he did Italian.
2. After the failure of the revolutionary uprisings of 1831 and 1848, the task of unification passed from Mazzini's republicans to Sardinia-Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II, and Cavour led it.
3. Through a tactful diplomatic alliance with France engineered by Cavour, Sardinia-Piedmont succeeded in defeating the Austrian forces in 1859.
4. His diplomacy, together with the campaign of Giuseppe Garibaldi's armed volunteers in South Italy in 1860, led to Victor Emmanuel II being proclaimed king of united Italy in 1861.
groundedIn: § 4 2 Italy Unified — the chapter's account of Chief Minister Cavour, his French alliance, the defeat of Austria in 1859 and the proclamation of Victor Emmanuel II in 1861

solution:
The Greek war of independence was the event that mobilised nationalist feelings among the educated elite across Europe.

1. Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century. The growth of revolutionary nationalism in Europe sparked off a struggle for independence among the Greeks, which began in 1821.
2. Nationalists in Greece got support from other Greeks living in exile, and also from many West Europeans who had sympathies for ancient Greek culture.
3. Poets and artists lauded Greece as the cradle of European civilisation and mobilised public opinion to support its struggle against a Muslim empire. The English poet Lord Byron organised funds and later went to fight in the war, where he died of fever in 1824.
4. The Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation.
groundedIn: § 3 The Age of Revolutions: 1830-1848 — the chapter's account of the Greek struggle from 1821, Lord Byron, and the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832

solution:
The Frankfurt parliament was the all-German National Assembly elected by the liberal middle classes in 1848.

1. In the German regions a large number of political associations, whose members were middle-class professionals, businessmen and prosperous artisans, came together in the city of Frankfurt and decided to vote for an all-German National Assembly.
2. On 18 May 1848, 831 elected representatives marched in a festive procession to take their places in the parliament, convened in the Church of St Paul.
3. They drafted a constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament.
4. When the deputies offered the crown on these terms to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, he rejected it and joined other monarchs to oppose the elected assembly.
5. The parliament was dominated by the middle classes, who resisted the demands of workers and artisans and so lost their support; as the opposition of the aristocracy and the military became stronger, troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband. Women had been denied suffrage rights in its election and were admitted only as observers in the visitors' gallery.
groundedIn: § 3 3 1848: The Revolution of the Liberals — the chapter's account of the Frankfurt parliament, the 831 representatives of 18 May 1848, Friedrich Wilhelm IV's refusal of the crown, and the disbanding of the assembly

stem: The role of women in nationalist struggles
solution:
Women took an active part in the liberal-nationalist struggles of the nineteenth century, but were denied the political rights those struggles demanded.

1. Large numbers of women had participated actively in the liberal movement over the years. They formed their own political associations, founded newspapers and took part in political meetings and demonstrations; Louise Otto-Peters, for example, founded a women's journal and subsequently a feminist political association.
2. The issue of extending political rights to women was a controversial one within the liberal movement itself.
3. Women were denied suffrage rights during the election of the Frankfurt Assembly, and when it convened in the Church of St Paul they were admitted only as observers to stand in the visitors' gallery.
4. Liberal 'equality before the law' did not mean universal suffrage. The Napoleonic Code reduced women to the status of a minor, subject to the authority of fathers and husbands, and throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries women and non-propertied men organised opposition movements demanding equal political rights.
5. Women were nevertheless central to the image of the nation: nations were personified as female figures such as Marianne and Germania, though the female form chosen did not stand for any particular woman in real life.
groundedIn: § 3 3 1848: The Revolution of the Liberals — its account of women's political associations, Louise Otto-Peters in Source C, and their admission to the Church of St Paul only as observers; § 2 2 What did Liberal Nationalism Stand for? — the exclusion of women from suffrage and their reduction to the status of a minor under the Napoleonic Code; § 5 Visualising the Nation — the female allegory standing for no woman in real life

subtopic: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation
stem: What steps did the French revolutionaries take to create a sense of collective identity among the French people?
solution:
The Revolution transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to a body of French citizens, and the revolutionaries then introduced measures and practices to make those citizens feel that they were one nation.

1. The ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen) were emphasised, stressing a united community enjoying equal rights under a constitution.
2. A new French flag, the tricolour, was chosen to replace the former royal standard.
3. The Estates General, elected by the body of active citizens, was renamed the National Assembly.
4. New hymns were composed, oaths taken and martyrs commemorated, all in the name of the nation.
5. A centralised administrative system was put in place, and it formulated uniform laws for all citizens within its territory.
6. Internal customs duties and dues were abolished and a uniform system of weights and measures was adopted.
7. Regional dialects were discouraged and French, as it was spoken and written in Paris, became the common language of the nation.
groundedIn: § 1 The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation — the chapter's list of the revolutionaries' measures: la patrie and le citoyen, the tricolour, the National Assembly, new hymns and oaths, a centralised administration, uniform weights and measures, and French as the common language

stem: Who were Marianne and Germania? What was the importance of the way in which they were portrayed?
solution:
Marianne and Germania were female allegories of the French and the German nation. Artists personified the nation as a female figure so that the abstract idea of the nation could be given a concrete form.

1. **Marianne** was christened with a popular Christian name, which underlined the idea of a people's nation. Her characteristics were drawn from those of Liberty and the Republic — the red cap, the tricolour and the cockade.
2. **Germania** became the allegory of the German nation. In visual representations she wears a crown of oak leaves, as the German oak stands for heroism.

Importance of the way they were portrayed:

1. The female form chosen did not stand for any particular woman in real life; it gave the nation a face people could recognise and identify with.
2. Every attribute carried a meaning — broken chains for being freed, the breastplate with an eagle for the strength of the German empire, the sword for readiness to fight, the olive branch around the sword for willingness to make peace, the black, red and gold tricolour for the flag of the liberal-nationalists of 1848, and the rays of the rising sun for the beginning of a new era.
3. Statues of Marianne were erected in public squares to remind the public of the national symbol of unity and to persuade them to identify with it, and her image was marked on coins and stamps, so the idea of the nation reached ordinary people in their daily life.
groundedIn: § 5 Visualising the Nation — the chapter's account of the female allegory, Marianne's red cap, tricolour and cockade, Germania's crown of oak leaves, the statues, coins and stamps, and the table of the meanings of the symbols in Box 3

subtopic: The Making of Germany and Italy
stem: Briefly trace the process of German unification.
solution:
1. Economic unity came first: in 1834 a customs union, the zollverein, was formed at the initiative of Prussia and joined by most of the German states. It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two, and a network of railways further harnessed economic interests to national unification.
2. Nationalist feelings were widespread among middle-class Germans, who in 1848 tried to unite the different regions of the German confederation into a nation-state governed by an elected parliament.
3. This liberal initiative to nation-building was repressed by the combined forces of the monarchy and the military, supported by the large landowners, called Junkers, of Prussia.
4. From then on Prussia took on the leadership of the movement for national unification. Its chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, was the architect of this process, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
5. Three wars over seven years — with Austria, Denmark and France — ended in Prussian victory and completed the process of unification.
6. In January 1871 the Prussian king, William I, was proclaimed German Emperor in a ceremony held in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.
7. The new state placed a strong emphasis on modernising the currency, banking and the legal and judicial systems, and Prussian measures and practices often became a model for the rest of Germany.
groundedIn: § 4 1 Germany – Can the Army be the Architect of a Nation? — the chapter's account of the repressed liberal initiative of 1848, Prussian leadership, Bismarck, the three wars and the proclamation of William I at Versailles in January 1871; § 2 2 What did Liberal Nationalism Stand for? — the zollverein of 1834 and the railways

subtopic: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation
stem: What changes did Napoleon introduce to make the administrative system more efficient in the territories ruled by him?
solution:
Through a return to monarchy Napoleon had destroyed democracy in France, but in the administrative field he incorporated revolutionary principles in order to make the whole system more rational and efficient.

1. The Civil Code of 1804, usually known as the Napoleonic Code, did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. This Code was exported to the regions under French control.
2. In the Dutch Republic, in Switzerland, in Italy and in Germany he simplified administrative divisions.
3. He abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues.
4. In the towns, guild restrictions were removed.
5. Transport and communication systems were improved.

As a result peasants, artisans, workers and new businessmen enjoyed a new-found freedom, and businessmen and small-scale producers began to realise that uniform laws, standardised weights and measures and a common national currency would facilitate the movement and exchange of goods and capital from one region to another.
groundedIn: § 1 The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation — the chapter's account of Napoleon's reforms in the territories he controlled: the Civil Code of 1804, simplified administrative divisions, the abolition of feudalism and serfdom, the removal of guild restrictions, and improved transport and communication

stem: Explain what is meant by the 1848 revolution of the liberals. What were the political, social and economic ideas supported by the liberals?
solution:
The 1848 revolution of the liberals was the revolution led by the educated middle classes that ran parallel to the revolts of the poor, unemployed and starving peasants and workers in the same year.

1. Events of February 1848 in France brought about the abdication of the monarch, and a republic based on universal male suffrage was proclaimed.
2. In Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, where independent nation-states did not yet exist, men and women of the liberal middle classes combined their demands for constitutionalism with national unification, taking advantage of the growing popular unrest to push for the creation of a nation-state on parliamentary principles.
3. Its chief expression was the Frankfurt parliament, convened in the Church of St Paul on 18 May 1848; when Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown it offered, troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband.
4. Conservative forces suppressed the liberal movements but could not restore the old order: serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg dominions and in Russia, and the Habsburg rulers granted more autonomy to the Hungarians in 1867.

Ideas supported by the liberals:

1. **Political** — an end to autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution, representative government through parliament, government by consent, freedom of the press and freedom of association.
2. **Social** — freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law. This did not amount to universal suffrage: the right to vote and to get elected was granted exclusively to property-owning men, and women were denied suffrage rights even in the election of the Frankfurt Assembly.
3. **Economic** — freedom of markets, the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital, and the inviolability of private property.
groundedIn: § 3 3 1848: The Revolution of the Liberals — the middle-class revolution of 1848, the February events in France, the Frankfurt parliament and the concessions that followed; § 2 2 What did Liberal Nationalism Stand for? — the political, social and economic content of liberalism, including limited suffrage and the freedom of markets

stem: Choose three examples to show the contribution of culture to the growth of nationalism in Europe.
solution:
Culture played an important role in creating the idea of the nation: art and poetry, stories and music helped express and shape nationalist feelings. Three examples:

1. **Romanticism.** Romantic artists and poets criticised the glorification of reason and science and focused instead on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings. Their effort was to create a sense of a shared collective heritage and a common cultural past as the basis of a nation.
2. **Folk culture.** The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people, das volk, and that it was through folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances that the true spirit of the nation, volksgeist, was popularised. Collecting and recording these forms of folk culture therefore became essential to the project of nation-building, and it also carried the nationalist message to audiences who were mostly illiterate.
3. **Language and music in Poland.** After Russian occupation the Polish language was forced out of schools and Russian was imposed everywhere. Following the crushed rebellion of 1831 the clergy used Polish for Church gatherings and all religious instruction, and many priests and bishops were jailed or sent to Siberia for refusing to preach in Russian, so the use of Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance. Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through his operas and music, turning folk dances like the polonaise and the mazurka into nationalist symbols.
groundedIn: § 3 1 The Romantic Imagination and National Feeling — the chapter's account of Romanticism, Herder's das volk and volksgeist, Karol Kurpinski's operas and the polonaise and mazurka, and the Polish language as a weapon of national resistance

subtopic: The Making of Germany and Italy
stem: Through a focus on any two countries, explain how nations developed over the nineteenth century.
solution:
**Germany**

1. Nationalist feelings were widespread among middle-class Germans, who in 1848 tried to unite the different regions of the German confederation into a nation-state governed by an elected parliament; this liberal initiative was repressed by the combined forces of the monarchy and the military, supported by the Junkers of Prussia.
2. Prussia then took on the leadership of the movement for national unification, with its chief minister Otto von Bismarck as the architect of the process, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
3. Three wars over seven years, with Austria, Denmark and France, ended in Prussian victory, and in January 1871 the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. The new state emphasised modernising the currency, banking and the legal and judicial systems.

**Italy**

1. Italy too had a long history of political fragmentation. In the middle of the nineteenth century it was divided into seven states, of which only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house; the north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre was ruled by the Pope and the southern regions were under the Bourbon kings of Spain. Even the Italian language had not acquired one common form.
2. During the 1830s Giuseppe Mazzini sought to put together a coherent programme for a unitary Italian Republic and formed the secret society Young Italy. The failure of the uprisings of 1831 and 1848 meant that the mantle fell on Sardinia-Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II to unify the Italian states through war.
3. Chief Minister Cavour engineered a tactful diplomatic alliance with France, through which Sardinia-Piedmont defeated the Austrian forces in 1859. In 1860 armed volunteers under Giuseppe Garibaldi marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and, with the support of the local peasants, drove out the Spanish rulers.
4. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy, though much of the Italian population, among whom rates of illiteracy were very high, remained unaware of liberal-nationalist ideology.

In both countries, therefore, the nation was made not by a popular democratic revolution but by a conservative state using war and diplomacy.
groundedIn: § 4 1 Germany – Can the Army be the Architect of a Nation? — the repression of the 1848 initiative, Prussian leadership under Bismarck, the three wars and the proclamation at Versailles; § 4 2 Italy Unified — the seven states, Mazzini and Young Italy, Cavour's alliance with France, Garibaldi's volunteers and the proclamation of Victor Emmanuel II in 1861

subtopic: The Making of Germany and Italy
stem: How was the history of nationalism in Britain unlike the rest of Europe?
solution:
In Britain the formation of the nation-state was not the result of a sudden upheaval or revolution, as elsewhere in Europe, but the result of a long-drawn-out process.

1. There was no British nation prior to the eighteenth century. The primary identities of the people who inhabited the British Isles were ethnic ones — English, Welsh, Scot or Irish — and all of these groups had their own cultural and political traditions.
2. As the English nation steadily grew in wealth, importance and power, it was able to extend its influence over the other nations of the islands. The English parliament, which had seized power from the monarchy in 1688, was the instrument through which a nation-state with England at its centre came to be forged.
3. The Act of Union of 1707 between England and Scotland resulted in the 'United Kingdom of Great Britain', which meant in effect that England was able to impose its influence on Scotland. The British parliament was henceforth dominated by its English members, Scotland's distinctive culture and political institutions were systematically suppressed, the Catholic clans of the Scottish Highlands suffered terrible repression, and the Highlanders were forbidden to speak their Gaelic language or wear their national dress and were forcibly driven out of their homeland in large numbers.
4. Ireland suffered a similar fate. The English helped the Protestants of Ireland to establish their dominance over a largely Catholic country and suppressed Catholic revolts; after the failed revolt led by Wolfe Tone and his United Irishmen in 1798, Ireland was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom in 1801.
5. A new 'British nation' was forged through the propagation of a dominant English culture — the Union Jack, the national anthem and the English language were actively promoted, and the older nations survived only as subordinate partners in this union.

So British nationalism was built by the gradual imposition of English dominance over its neighbours, and not, as in Germany or Italy, by a nationalist movement uniting a fragmented people.
groundedIn: § 4 3 The Strange Case of Britain — the chapter's account of the long-drawn-out process, the ethnic identities before the eighteenth century, the parliament of 1688, the Act of Union of 1707, the repression of the Scottish Highlanders, Wolfe Tone's failed revolt and the incorporation of Ireland in 1801, and the symbols of the new Britain

stem: Why did nationalist tensions emerge in the Balkans?
solution:
The Balkans was the most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871, because by then nationalism had become a narrow creed with limited ends and the great powers were manipulating the nationalist aspirations of subject peoples for imperialist ends.

1. The Balkans was a region of geographical and ethnic variation, comprising modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as the Slavs.
2. A large part of the region was under the control of the Ottoman Empire. The spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism, together with the disintegration of that empire, made the region very explosive; Ottoman attempts at modernisation and internal reform had very little success, and one by one its European subject nationalities broke away and declared independence.
3. The Balkan peoples based their claims for independence or political rights on nationality, and used history to prove that they had once been independent but had subsequently been subjugated by foreign powers. They therefore thought of their struggles as attempts to win back a long-lost independence.
4. The Balkan states were fiercely jealous of each other, and each hoped to gain more territory at the expense of the others, so the area became an area of intense conflict.
5. The Balkans also became the scene of big power rivalry. Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary, already in intense rivalry over trade and colonies as well as naval and military might, were each keen on countering the hold of the others over the Balkans and extending their own control.

This led to a series of wars in the region and finally to the First World War.
groundedIn: § 6 Nationalism and Imperialism — the chapter's account of the Balkans after 1871: its ethnic variation and Slav inhabitants, Ottoman disintegration, claims based on nationality and history, rivalry between the Balkan states, and the rivalry of Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary that ended in the First World War
